title: The router's gradient
goal:
With top-1 routing, the argmax has no gradient. Yet the router still learns, because the expert output is multiplied by the gate value $p_i(x)$ (Section 2.1: "the gate value $p_i(x)$ in Equation 2 permits differentiability of the router"). For one token routed to expert $i$, the layer output is

$$y = p_i(x) \, E_i(x), \qquad E_i(x) = W_i^{\top} x.$$

Write `switch_forward(x, Wr, W)` and `switch_backward(cache, dy)` for a layer of $N$ linear experts.

- `x`: `(T, d)`. `Wr`: `(d, N)`. `W`: `(N, d, d_out)`, where `W[i]` is expert $i$'s weight matrix.
- `switch_forward` returns `(y, cache)` with `y` of shape `(T, d_out)`.
- `switch_backward` takes `dy`, the gradient of the loss with respect to `y`, and returns `(dWr, dW)`, the gradients with respect to `Wr` and `W`. Skip the gradient with respect to `x`.

The tests compare your gradients with finite differences, then train the layer on a toy task where four clusters of inputs need four different linear maps. A single linear map can't fit the task.
hints: Forward: `h = x @ Wr`, `p = softmax(h)`, `i = argmax(p)`, `g = p[t, i]`, `out = x[t] @ W[i[t]]`, `y = g * out`.

Gradient to the gate: $\partial L / \partial g = \sum_k dy_k \cdot out_k$. It reaches the logits through the softmax. Only the chosen entry of $p$ receives it, so $dp = g' \cdot e_i$ (a one-hot vector).
Softmax backward: $dh = p \odot (dp - \sum_j dp_j p_j)$ for each token.
Gradient to the expert: $dW_i = \sum_{t:\, idx_t = i} x_t \, (g_t \cdot dy_t)^{\top}$. A token only updates its own expert.
